item.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
item.description:
Source: github.com

Hi all

I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.

Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.

So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!

It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.

So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.

It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.

During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).

You can check out a demo video on the site of me singing (warning given) here: https://singonkey.app

The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.

The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.

It’s still weak in a few places:

- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out

- sometimes it gets a note an octave off

- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point

- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on you

Would love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!

Top Comment:

I have thoughts about this pedagologically. I think these kinds of tools can be helpful, but the number of rhythm students I have seen who need to break out of the dependence on a visual metronome is rough.

Part of the struggle is really listening to yourself, and learning how to pick up on your own mistakes.

I hope the tool is helpful, and I hope I don't sound too curmudgeonly when I say don't let the time making and maintaining tools for practice detract from the most important thing, the ur-tool of all learning: more practice.

(Ask me how I know! A common trap for programmers!)

item.title: Remove pgrust: the entry is cheating (per-query kernels and result caching)
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

Hi! I'm the creator of pgrust. Let me explain what happened.

For the most part, the actual accusations are false. This submission was an earlier version of pgrust 0.4 called pgrust 0.4-preview. We just open-sourced a newer version called pgrust 0.4-beta yesterday, and you can fully audit it here[0]. Rather than contest the accusations on GitHub, we figured it would be easier to complete pgrust 0.4 and open-source it to show that we're being honest. You can also verify what I'm saying yourself against the 0.4-preview binary we submitted to ClickBench here[1]. I don't have a way to prove this is the exact binary submitted, but if ClickHouse provided the SHA of the binary they tested against, it would match.

The three main accusations boil down to: 1) We used handwritten code optimized against each query in the benchmark, 2) We cached the results between query runs, and 3) We didn't support queries outside of the 43 ClickBench queries.

First, we did not use handwritten queries. The code Alexey pointed out does not run during the benchmark. The design of 0.4 relies on a JIT compiler that compiles your SQL to a Lisp-based intermediate representation that we call Gravity IR that we then convert to x86 and ARM assembly. While developing 0.4, I wrote handwritten code against the IR for benchmarking purposes. The idea was that if queries written in our IR are fast, and we can compile good enough IR fast, then our new query engine will be fast. This is also the reason the directory those "kernels" are in is called "irprobe" - it was a probe of our IR to make sure it was fast. Our 0.4-preview submission went through the pipeline: SQL query -> Gravity IR -> assembly.

Second, the "result-cache" Alexey observed is the result of a cache we use to cache which predicates match which strings in our dictionaries we use for dictionary compression. Alexey wasn't aware of this cache and assumed we were just caching the query results. On ClickBench you are allowed to use caches like this that hold intermediate data[2]. ClickHouse has its own cache similar to this called the Condition Cache[3]. In our newest submission, we were upfront about all the caching we do and how to disable each cache[4].

The third claim that we didn't support other queries outside of the 43 ClickBench queries is partially false, but does have some ground to it. As I said before, pgrust 0.4-preview was an early version of pgrust 0.4. Once our new JIT compiler supported enough SQL to handle the ClickBench queries, we decided to submit it to ClickBench. AFAIK, ClickBench has no rules about how much SQL you need to support. On top of that, we did ship that we did ship 0.4-preview with our old query engine. It would have been a two-line change to fall back to it and support a much broader set of queries outside what our new engine could support. Those queries would still be fast, but not quite as fast as our new engine was. Our new 0.4-beta release does now support all Postgres SQL (minus some bugs around CTEs and MERGE)

To sum up, pgrust 0.4-preview was an early build of pgrust 0.4 while it was in development. It was a real query engine and actually executed queries. I acknowledge that we submitted it prematurely, when it supported a narrow set of SQL, and we should have ensured broader SQL coverage before submitting it. With our new submission that solves these problems, and we're hoping for pgrust to be reinstated. If there's anything off about the submission, please point it out and we're happy to fix it.

[1] https://pgrust.com/downloads/archive/2026-09-clickbench-snap...

[2] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/blob/main/README.md

[3] https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/performance/ca...

[4] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/pull/2751

item.title: Jank – The native Clojure dialect with seamless C++ interop
item.description:
Source: jank-lang.org

Top Comment:

Hey folks. I'm the jank creator.

jank is a full Clojure dialect with unprecedented C++ interop. Unlike the OG Lisp/C++ combo, Clasp, there is no bridge API necessary for registering C++ functions, types, or values. jank can seamlessly interop with any C++ by just including the headers. Interop includes template instantiations, overload resolution (implicit conversions, ADL, etc), exception throwing/catching, virtual function calls, and literally everything else.

jank _is C++_, since it compiles to C++ and uses the C++ type system. It ships with a Clang-powered JIT C++ compiler to make all of the REPL goodies work. jank also improves upon the C++ build ecosystem with Cargo-like tooling.

This means you can use jank to make C++ native applications, you can embed jank into your C++ applications, or you can even use jank to just write portable Clojure libraries that people use from other Clojure dialects.

We're still in alpha right now, so things are a bit unstable. We're targeting a more stable beta release in January. The best way you can help is to try jank out and report every friction point you have on Slack, Discord, or Github.

I've been working on jank for several years. It is not vibe-coded.
